title: Pokémon Center Online designates first Pokémon items that will require Japanese ID card to buy
description: Fans will need to be residents of Japan in order to buy these items from the Pokémon Center Online. Scalping is becoming an increasingly large problem for the Pokémon franchise, and the latest move by the Pokémon Company to clamp down on the practice is a new system that requires a Japanese government-issued ID card […]
content:
Fans will need to be residents of Japan in order to buy these items from the Pokémon Center Online.

Scalping is becoming an increasingly large problem for the Pokémon franchise, and the latest move by the Pokémon Company to clamp down on the practice is a new system that requires a Japanese government-issued ID card for making certain purchases through the Pokémon Center Online store. As unveiled last month, the system works in tandem with the Digital Identification App, an app created by the Digital Agency (part of the prime minster’s cabinet) and the My Number Card, a government-issued ID card that’s also used in the administration of social services such as health insurance and social security/national pension payments.

The Pokémon Center Online has now announced the first items which will require shoppers to prove their identity through the Digital App, with four Pokémon Card Game items designated for such protection, all of them part of the Pokémon Card Game’s 30th Celebration series and scheduled to go on sale next month. The restricted items are:

● Pokémon Card Game Mega Expansion Pack 30th Celebration Box (7,200 yen [US$46])
● Pokémon Card Game Mega 30th Celebration Futuristic Box (27,500 yen)
● Pokémon Card Game Mega 30th Celebration Espeon and Umbreon Premium Deck Set (6,200 yen)
● Pokémon Card Game Mega 30th Celebration Card Set (9-type complete set) (10,800 yen)

▼ The Futuristic Box is a bundle that includes two guaranteed Pikachu ex promo cards, card shields, a deck case, and a play mat, and a display case, among other items.

▼ The Pokémon Card Game Mega 30th Celebration Espeon and Umbreon Premium Deck Set features two ex cards of Espeon and Umbron each, part of two separate decks with a grand total of 60 cards.

Now, if you’re wondering how non-residents of Japan can get a My Number Card and use the Digital Identification App, the answer is that they can’t. So in requiring verification through the app, the Pokémon Center Online is effectively restricting sales of the affected items to Japanese residents only.

That’s an unhappy side effect, but odds are the Pokémon Company imagines that legitimate foreign fans aren’t likely to be getting shut out of making the purchases. While visiting tourists do indeed drop a lot of cash on Pokémon stuff in Japan, merch such as Pokémon plushies, T-shirts, and even Happy Meal toys are the big draws for fans from overseas. Pokémon cards sold in Japan explain the card’s capabilities in Japanese text only, so the language barrier makes them of limited appeal or utility for foreign fans who’re actually interested in using them to play the game, which would suggest that foreign shoppers who are buying and limited-edition cards/card sets are doing so for some other purpose. On the other hand, it could be that the Pokémon Center Online’s decision to require use of the Digital Identification App is simply because it’s Japan’s most extensive domestic platform for electronic identity verification, thus making it the most easily available infrastructure for tracking repeat/bulk purchases by the same person, regardless of nationality.

▼ The Pokémon Card Game Mega 30th Celebration Card Sets come in nine versions, with a guaranteed set of cards representing a single generation’s starter Pokémon, a display stand, and two packs of cards.

It’s not clear whether physical Pokémon Center stores in Japan will also require buyers to use the Digital Identification App/a My Number Card in order to make purchases. No other retailers currently have any such requirements in place, but may enact their own sort of anti-scalping methods.

Pre-orders for the restricted item open on August 10 for the Pokémon Card Game Mega Expansion Pack 30th Celebration Box, 30th Celebration Futuristic Box, and 30th Celebration Espeon and Umbreon Premium Deck Set with a slated shipping date of September 15, with the respective dates for the Pokémon Card Game Mega 30th Celebration Card Sets are August 28 and October 15.

title: Toyota Museum’s international retro vehicle parade returns to Aichi this autumn
description: Cruise over to Moricoro Park for 120 vintage cars or apply and show off your own pre-1997 classic. The Toyota Motor Corporation is a household name in much of the world for being the largest automobile manufacturer on a global scale, but has also had a big impact back at home. Rooted deep in Aichi […]
content:
Cruise over to Moricoro Park for 120 vintage cars or apply and show off your own pre-1997 classic.

The Toyota Motor Corporation is a household name in much of the world for being the largest automobile manufacturer on a global scale, but has also had a big impact back at home. Rooted deep in Aichi Prefecture, the city of Koromo renamed itself Toyota City in 1959 to honor the company, its primary engine of growth. Just down the road from the city, in neighboring Nagakute City, sits the Toyota Automobile Museum, an institution that seeks to preserve global car history across every manufacturer and era, well beyond Toyota’s own lineage. That’s not to be confused with the nearby Toyota Kaikan Museum that focuses on Toyota products and services, as well as the latest Toyota and Lexus models.

On November 15, the 36th Toyota Automobile Museum Classic Car Festival makes its return, promising an unforgettable experience celebrating automotive history at Expo 2005 Aichi Commemorative Park, also known as Morocoro Park, which also plays host to the fantastical Ghibli Park.

The festival starts with a 14-kilometer (8.7-mile) parade featuring between 100 to 120 preserved classic cars rolling through public streets, starting at 7:00 a.m. from the museum.

Once the parade arrives at Moricoro Park, you can take a closer look at the vintage Japanese and international gems. Owners of the cars will be mingling around looking to chat about their beloved rides, sometimes wearing period attire, or setting up some custom memory panels to explain more about the car’s history. With food trucks, local booths, and the lush park grounds, it all makes for a fantastic day out for friends and family.

While official spectator entrance details for 2026 are still pending, looking back at the 35th festival, which was held in spring 2025, admission to the exhibition was completely free, so if you’re a lover of classic cars, you’re likely to be in for some budget-friendly fun.

If you happen to own a classic car in Japan, it’s possible to get in on the action yourself. Any Japanese or imported cars produced in or before 1996 (excluding motorcycles) are eligible, but vehicles must be street-legal and in a driveable state on the day of the event. Propellers and flotation devices are not proof of roadworthiness, no matter how phantasmagorical a machine it may be.

Applications for participation open from August 5 to August 15 via the official Toyota Automobile Museum website. If selected for one of the limited spots available, the participation fee is 5,000 yen (US$31.38), which covers the official parade number, a commemorative badge, and event pamphlet.

Whether you want to take a trip down memory lane or are in the mood to experience some history, you won’t be needing 1.21 gigawatts to feel the nostalgia, just head on down to Moricoro Park this November.

title: Tokyo’s Haneda Airport airlines announce stricter luggage check-in deadline for domestic flights
description: JAL and ANA among carriers to start requiring earlier baggage check-in very soon. The convenience of using Haneda Airport isn’t just its close proximity to downtown Tokyo, it’s also how easy the station is to access by train. There’s a station right in the basement of the building, with elevators that will take you right […]
content:
JAL and ANA among carriers to start requiring earlier baggage check-in very soon.

The convenience of using Haneda Airport isn’t just its close proximity to downtown Tokyo, it’s also how easy the station is to access by train. There’s a station right in the basement of the building, with elevators that will take you right from the platform up into the departure lobbies, and when you add in how punctual and reliable Japan’s rail networks are, it can be easy to assume you don’t need to build much buffer space into your schedule when you’re heading to Haneda to catch a flight.

However, several airlines that fly out of Haneda, including JAL and ANA, have put out a reminder that there’s a limit to how close you can cut things, as they’ve announced that they’ll be instituting stricter deadlines for checking in bags for domestic flights, and they’ll be going into effect very soon.

Under the new policy, JAL, ANA, Air Do, StarFlyer, Solaseed Air, and Japan Transocean Air will be moving back their baggage check-in deadline by an additional 10 minutes, with the new deadline being 30 minutes before the flight’s departure time. Note that this is not a suggested time, but a hard cutoff, implying that passengers with bags to check who show up at the counter with less than 30 minutes to spare before departure will be faced with a choice between missing their flight or leaving their bags behind.

In addition to the six airlines mentioned above, Skymark says that while it is currently sticking with its baggage check-in cutoff of 20 minutes before departure, it will be monitoring the situation and moving up the deadline if it becomes necessary to do so. All seven airlines have also issued statements reminding passengers that their flight’s scheduled departure time indicates the time at which the plane is slated pull away from the gate, and so passengers are expected to be boarded at least 10 minutes prior to departure.

At the moment, the policy change applies only to domestic routes, but with the change coming as part of a renewed effort to maintain punctual takeoff times, there’s a chance that JAL and ANA will be keeping an eye on whether or not similar changes are necessary to keep its international flights on time. So again, while it can be tempting to time you arrival at Haneda so that you roll up at the last possible moment before you need to be there, the wise thing to do is to actually arrive a little earlier, especially since there’s usually something cool to see at the airport.

title: Sanrio characters join forces with your favorite Japanese snack mascots as prizes at Family Mart

The convenience store chain offers the summer’s most kawaii collab by bringing 26 characters from different worlds together.

Major Japanese convenience store chain Family Mart is celebrating its 45th anniversary in September with some of the cutest, most recognizable mascots out there!

Buying eligible products will allow you to receive promotional prizes, and saving up stamps from showing your FamiPay app at the time of purchase will earn you entries in a lottery for more prizes. Plus, there will be limited-time Sanrio goods for anyone to purchase.

First, let’s focus on the promotional prizes you can receive with purchase of two eligible products. How do you know which products are eligible for the campaign? That’s easy–just look for this bright green label on applicable items in the store:

The prizes will arrive in two rounds and in two different forms–acrylic keychains and cloth drawstring pouches–as detailed below. They will be randomly distributed to customers making qualified purchases.

Round 1 began on August 4 at 10 a.m. and with eight acrylic keychains.

Round 2 will also have cloth drawstring pouches. The pouches come in a pink version and a green version, with six of the collaborative designs on the former and seven on the latter.

Second, let’s take a look at the fabulous prizes you could win by saving up enough stamps to enter the prize lotteries. To gain stamps, simply display your FamiPay app while making an eligible purchase. Each purchase will grant you one stamp. You can enter three different lotteries depending on the number of stamps you’ve saved up which each result in a different prize. This part of the campaign runs from August 4 through August 31, and you can enter the lottery between August 4 and September 4.

We have to say–we think that Family Mart really hit the kawaii jackpot with this latest campaign. We can’t wait to get snacking and packing prizes of our favorite mascots!

title: Coco’s Japan is very confident in their chilled ramen, but should they be? [Taste test]
description: Premium-priced hiyashi chuka comes to the American coffee shop’s Japanese branches. With the summer heat hitting Japan in full force, it’s time to look for ways to stay cool however you can, even when you’re eating, and recently that search took us to Coco’s to try their chilled ramen. And just to be clear, when […]
content:
Premium-priced hiyashi chuka comes to the American coffee shop’s Japanese branches.

With the summer heat hitting Japan in full force, it’s time to look for ways to stay cool however you can, even when you’re eating, and recently that search took us to Coco’s to try their chilled ramen. And just to be clear, when we say “Coco’s,” we’re not talking about Japanese curry rice restaurant chain Coco Ichibanya. No, we’re actually talking about Coco’s, the American coffee shop that also has branches in Japan.

In its home country, Coco’s is known for reliably tasty, but not necessarily adventurous, American fare. Bacon-and-egg breakfasts, burgers with French fries, slices of apple pie, those kinds of things. But as is sometimes the case when restaurant chains from the U.S. cross the Pacific, Coco’s Japan has a more varied, and also upscale, menu, and right now that includes hiyashi chuka, a chilled ramen dish that Japan loves eating in the summer.

Not only is Coco’s Japan serving chilled ramen, they’re very confident in its quality, as they’re asking 1,419 yen (US$8.75) for it. It’s possible to find hiyashi chuka for close to half that price at casual restaurants, so in setting the price that high, Coco’s has set the bar pretty high for itself.

Coco’s does offer some special ingredients to justify its premium pricing, though. For starters, the standard hiyashi chuka toppings are egg, cucumber, tomato, and ham. Coco’s replaces that last one, though, with roast beef, a much fancier ingredient.

You also get some nice, big shrimp…

…wakame (seaweed)…

…and even okra, which is something we’d never encountered in hiyashi chuka before this.

The presentation is quite beautiful, and we rotated our bowl around to get a good, appreciative look at the chilled ramen from every angle. Having passed the visual test, it was time to move on to the taste test, performed by our Japanese-language writer Takashi Harada, and he’s happy to report that Coco’s hiyashi chuka tastes every bit as good as it looks!

There are quite a few different flavors involved in hiyashi chuka, with even the chilled, vinegary broth having both sweet and sour elements to it. Too much of any one aspect can make the entire meal feel off, but everything here works perfectly together. Takashi was especially impressed by the quality of the tomatoes and okra, which had no unpleasant acidity or bitterness, so much so that he’s now convinced that okra can be a viable addition to the dish. Likewise, roast beef turned out to be an ingenious addition, especially with the little dab of sweet sauce that Coco’s applies to the meat.

The noodles are excellent too, thin and with just the right amount of firmness. And if you want your chilled ramen to still bring some heat to your taste buds, you get a side dish with some very hot spicy mustard if you want to mix it in.

So Coco’s hiyashi chuka isn’t just better than one might expect, but, simply put, very good hiyashi chuka. If you’re looking for something to both fill you up and cool you off this summer, it’s very much worth its price…and if noodles aren’t your thing, they’ve got other traditionally Japanese ways to cool off too.

title: Starbucks Japan to open Shinkansen platform stores at Kyoto and Nagoya stations
description: New stores add a fresh taste and aroma to high-speed travel on Japan’s busiest bullet train route. One of the joys of Shinkansen travel is being able to bring your own food and drinks on board. However, with the high-speed rail service being famously punctual, you don’t always have time to pick up what you […]
content:
New stores add a fresh taste and aroma to high-speed travel on Japan’s busiest bullet train route.

One of the joys of Shinkansen travel is being able to bring your own food and drinks on board. However, with the high-speed rail service being famously punctual, you don’t always have time to pick up what you need when rushing to get your train.

It’s a pre-departure dilemma that Starbucks is now seeking to address by opening stores right at the platform. Late last year, the chain broke new ground by opening its first-ever Starbucks on a Shinkansen platform, and now it’s announced plans to open additional stores at two more major stations on the line.

The first location opened on JR Shin-Yokohama Station’s downbound Platform 11 last November and quickly proved popular with travellers. However, demand also led to queues and longer wait times, prompting Starbucks to temporarily close the store in April to improve its ordering system before reopening in June.

The chain now appears confident that it has a good working model from which to expand operations, and so has announced that the “travel Starbucks experience” will soon be arriving at Shinkansen platforms at JR Kyoto Station and JR Nagoya Station, with the new locations scheduled to open from next year.

While Starbucks hasn’t shared any details about the exact platforms where the new stores will be located, or when in 2027 they will open, the existing Shin-Yokohama branch gives us a pretty good idea of what we can expect.

Rather than being full-scale cafes with chairs and tables, the new stores look set to be takeaway kiosks – the Shin-Yokohama Shinkansen platform store measures just 13.9 square metres (150 square feet) – with no seating at all.

Designed for travellers with trains to catch, the new kiosk-style Starbucks focuses on speed, serving a limited menu of freshly brewed coffee, including decaf options, and a small selection of snacks. Orders are placed via a touchscreen terminal, and the store is entirely cashless.

The new Kyoto and Nagoya platform branches look set to follow the same formula, so Shinkansen passengers can easily squeeze in a Starbucks order before stepping on the train. With the Shin-Yokohama platform branch recently receiving its own unique digital stamp in Starbucks’ “My Store Passport” app feature, which allows visitors to collect a virtual souvenir of their visit, the Kyoto and Nagoya branches are likely to receive their own stamps when they open too.

▼ The Shin-Yokohama stamp highlights its location in Kanagawa Prefecture.

With all three platforms servicing the Tokaido Shinkansen, Japan’s most popular route that runs from Tokyo to Kyoto and Shin-Osaka, we wouldn’t be surprised if a Starbucks Shinkansen stamp rally might soon be in the works. For the chain that gave us 47 prefecture-exclusive Frappuccinos and a Discovery Series that celebrates local regions and traditions, we have a feeling that the new Shinkansen platform stores are just the start of the journey for the “travel Starbucks experience”.

title: Aichi city throws year-long 20th birthday bash for giant beckoning cat statue, Hello Kitty invited
description: The 20th birthday of a local legend calls for collaborations with Hello Kitty, Chubu Centrair International Airport, and 15 local businesses. March 28, 2027 will mark 20 years to the day when the city of Tokoname in Aichi Prefecture erected a giant manekineko (beckoning cat) statue affectionately named Tokonyan. At 3.8 meters (4.2 yards) tall and […]
content:
The 20th birthday of a local legend calls for collaborations with Hello Kitty, Chubu Centrair International Airport, and 15 local businesses.

March 28, 2027 will mark 20 years to the day when the city of Tokoname in Aichi Prefecture erected a giant manekineko (beckoning cat) statue affectionately named Tokonyan. At 3.8 meters (4.2 yards) tall and 6.3 meters wide, Tokonyan is a popular photo spot near the entrance to the Pottery Footpath (Yakimono Sanpomichi), a local sightseeing spot that highlights the city’s rich pottery heritage and traditional Tokoname ware along with historical kilns, brick chimneys, and other related landmarks. Birthday celebrations are already underway as the city has dubbed the time between August 1, 2026 and July 31, 2027 as Tokonyan’s 20th Anniversary Year.

Such a big birthday milestone calls for special party favors, and thankfully some big names have signed on for the haul. As of August 1, three collaborative goods with Sanrio star Hello Kitty are being sold at the Tokoname Tourism Association.

▼ Felines unite!

▼ Embroidered towel / 660 yen (US$4.19)

▼ Acrylic keychain / 660 yen

▼ Sticker / 550 yen

In addition, beginning on August 15, collaborative merch with the nearby Chubu Centrair International Airport will also make their debut at the Association.

▼ The airport’s own mascot is called “Mysterious Traveler Fu.”

▼ Clear folder / 550 yen

▼ Magnet / 550 yen

▼ Sticker / 440 yen

What’s probably the biggest sign of Tokoname’s love for Tokonyan, however, is the fact that 15 local businesses are also offering limited-time collaborative menus and products (pictured below) for the duration of the year-long celebration.

▼ Products include Tokonyan-themed cream bread, parfaits, and cider, to name just a few.

Finally, visitors can snap a special photo next to an illuminated Tokonyan during two specified timeframes: December 18-25 (100 days before its birthday) and March 19-April 4 (its birthday week).

▼ Any photo taken then will become a special keepsake for sure.

As an extra bonus, a social media campaign will also begin on February 22 (Cat Day in Japan) and last through April 30, during which time users can follow Tokoname Tourism Association’s official Instagram or X/Twitter accounts and post a message celebrating the anniversary using hashtag ＃とこにゃん20周年. They’ll then automatically be entered into a lottery to win some fantastic prizes such as Tokonyan merch or local Tokoname specialty products.

It’s hard to imagine that there’s any other place in Japan that loves its local manekineko just as much–but we’ve got a strong contender.

title: Final Fantasy plushie shoulder bags are fuzzy and functional [Photos]
description: Chocobo, Moogle, and two more Final Fantasy mascot creatures want to go with you on your outside-the-house adventures. content:
Chocobo, Moogle, and two more Final Fantasy mascot creatures want to go with you on your outside-the-house adventures.

Final Fantasy’s Chocobo and Moogle are always welcome presences, so any fan of the Square Enix video game series would be happy to have these cubic forms of the cute creatures gracing their home, right?

Ah, but Final Fantasy is, above all else, a story of adventure. So while it’s nice to know you have a Chocobo or Moogle waiting for you when you get home, something really true to the spirit of the series would be a Chocobo or Moogle who’ll go with you when you while you’re out in the field, and these guys can do that too!

These aren’t just ordinary plushies. They’re “Final Fantasy Fuzzy Slings,” with an attachable strap so that they can function as shoulder bags.

The boxy proportions are more than mere quirky aesthetics. To use their full name, these are the Final Fantasy Fluffy Sling Deck Boxes. Open up the flap, and inside is a deck case, sized to hold 145 cards from the Final Fantasy Trading Card Game.

「#FFTCG」より、『ファイナルファンタジーX』25周年を記念したスペシャルコレクションが登場！これまでに発売された人気カードに加え、ブースターパック至福の永劫に収録された高レアリティカードもラインアップ。作品の世界観を感じられる特別なコレクションです。#FF10https://t.co/1xKYpVjDOj pic.twitter.com/fD6C82OkGC

— スクウェア・エニックス e-STORE (@SQEX_eSTORE) July 31, 2026

However, just like you can take the shoulder strap on and off, the deck case is removable too. So if you’re not going to be engaging in any card battles while you’re out and about, you can slide the case out and use the bag to store whatever key items you actually do need for the day.

Also part of the Fuzzy Sling lineup is Cactaur, whose soft-to-the-touch fabric is a nice change of place from being pelted by his trademark 1,000 Needles attack.

And rounding out the quartet is Fat Cat, the newest entry to the franchise out of the four creatures here, but one who’s still much-loved, especially within the Final Fantasy XIV fandom.

All of the Fuzzy Slings are priced at 7,590 yen (US$48) and available for pre-order through the Square Enix E-store here, with shipping scheduled for late November.

title: Akita Kanto Festival, one of Japan’s most spectacular summer festivals, gets an anime twist this year

content:
Towering lanterns, traditional balancing skills, and a special anime collaboration make this an unforgettable Japanese festival experience.

There are many famous summer festivals in Japan, but the Akita Kanto Festival is one of the most magical and awe-inspiring. Held in Akita City every August, this festival features fantastical lanterns that sway to represent rice stalks, held aloft by people who balance the enormous structures on their hips, shoulders, palm, chins and foreheads in an amazing display of dexterity and teamwork that draws thousands of spectators.

Now the festival is drawing more than spectators, it’s drawing anime characters too, with the popular manga and anime series Golden Kamuy making an appearance at the event. This tie-up with the festival is particularly apt as Akita Prefecture is the birthplace of Genjirou Tanigaki, one of the characters from the series, and the region’s history and culture have strong links to the world depicted in the story.

▼ Anime characters balancing the lanterns on their forehead and shoulder, just as performers do at the real-world festival.

The event, which runs until 26 August, consists of two main parts: an exhibition of character panels featuring newly drawn visuals and a pop-up shop, all being held at Atrion, a multi-purpose complex located about a five-minute walk from JR Akita Station. Fans of the series will want to head to Atrion during the day so they can view the large character panels, featuring the cast dressed in Kanto Festival outfits.

The displays are impressive in scale, with the characters appearing almost life-sized. Combined with the Kanto lantern poles, some of the displays reache more than three metres (9.8 feet) tall, recreating the awesome sight of the real-world festival.

The characters of Sugimoto, Asirpa, and Shiraishi are shown as members of the “hayashikata”, the musicians who provide the festival’s traditional sounds.

While the people who physically balance the Kanto poles, known as “sashite”, have traditionally been men, women have participated as musicians since the late Showa period (1926-1989). These days, visitors to the actual festival can see many female performers taking part in this important role.

▼  Lanterns decorated with Golden Kamuy character names recreate the look of the famous Kanto displays.

The same floor is also home to a pop-up shop selling collaboration goods, including acrylic stands, keychains, T-shirts, towels, and other items featuring the festival theme.

▼ The designs capture the personalities of the characters perfectly, and the Akita dog costumes are incredibly cute.

The Golden Kamuy event is a great way to get into the mood of the festival, which is best enjoyed at night, when the lanterns light up the sky as they tower over the crowds, swaying from side to side, and occasionally crashing down by accident before being picked up again. The night event, which runs from 3-6 August, is worth hanging around for, and while you wait there are plenty of things to see and do around Akita City.

▼ Just across from Atrion is Senshu Park, a public park built on the former grounds of Kubota Castle.

During summer, the park’s moat is covered in blooming lotus flowers, creating a beautiful sight that feels worlds away from the busy city streets.

Visitors should also keep an eye out for Akita’s famous summer treat, babahera ice cream. The colourful ice cream is shaped into rose-like designs by skilled vendors using quick movements that are almost like a performance.

During the day there are some events to give you a taste of what’s to come at night, and when you see the Kanto poles in person you can get a sense of why the festival is considered a true test of skill. The largest poles, known as “Owaka”, measure around 12 metres (39 feet) long and weigh approximately 50 kilograms (110 pounds). Moving them into position requires teamwork, but the real challenge begins when performers balance them on different parts of their bodies.

The techniques, known as “myogi”, include balancing the pole on the palm, shoulder, forehead, and hip. Watching performers hold the massive structures steady using various parts of their body is an incredibly impressive sight to behold.

▼ The hip technique is considered one of the more advanced moves, requiring years of experience and incredible body control.

When darkness falls, the main streets stretching from JR Akita Station toward Akita City Hall are transformed into a pedestrian-only festival area.

One by one, the giant Kanto poles are raised into the night sky, and the warm glow of hundreds of lanterns begins to float above the streets as traditional music plays and performers move with careful concentration beneath the towering displays. From a distance, the lanterns look like stars drifting through the city, while up close, the skill and concentration of the performers creates a completely different kind of spectacle.

Sometimes the poles collide, and sometimes they fall, giving you a sense of just how heavy and difficult they are to control. Sometimes, performers manage to save a pole from falling, regaining control at the last minute, eliciting cheers of delight and applause from the crowd.

Beneath the beauty of the lanterns lies years of skill and team effort, and watching it all unfold up close is all part of the magic of the festival.

At the western end of the festival venue near Akita City Hall, visitors can also find a food village filled with local specialties, including Yokote yakisoba, Hinai chicken ramen, and Akita sake.

This year also saw a new addition to the festivities, with a drone show filling the sky above the city. Unlike fireworks, drones can perform directly above urban areas, acting like a giant moving canvas above the festival crowds.

▼ One of the cutest displays was the giant representation of an Akita dog, a symbol of prefectural pride.

Towering lanterns, incredible performers, local food, and a touch of Golden Kamuy magic makes this year’s Akita Kanto Festival one of the best events of the year. The festival is much more than a parade, it’s a display of skill and a traditional performing art, and it’s easy to see why it remains one of Japan’s most unforgettable summer celebrations.

title: U.S. government reportedly planning to close Nagoya consulate
description: Move would leave Japan’s fourth-largest city without consular services. With a population of roughly 2.3 million people, Nagoya is the fourth-largest city in Japan. It also holds an extremely important position in Japanese industry and its connections to the global economy, by nature of being the closest major city to the head office of Toyota […]
content:
Move would leave Japan’s fourth-largest city without consular services.

With a population of roughly 2.3 million people, Nagoya is the fourth-largest city in Japan. It also holds an extremely important position in Japanese industry and its connections to the global economy, by nature of being the closest major city to the head office of Toyota and many of the automakers factories and suppliers.

Nevertheless, the U.S. government is planning to close its consulate in Nagoya, according to a report from Reuters citing sources who spoke under condition of anonymity.

According to the report, the U.S. State Department has sent notices to multiple congressional committees informing them of its intent to close the Nagoya consulate, as well as the U.S. embassy in Granada, consulates in Canada (Winnipeg) and Indonesia (Medan), and an embassy branch office in Cameroon (Douala). The downsizing does not appear to be tied to any diplomatic disagreements and to instead be a cost-cutting move by the U.S. government.

Shutting down the Nagoya consulate would leave the full embassy in Tokyo and and the consulate in Osaka as the nearest alternatives, both of which are roughly and hour and a half away from Nagoya by Shinkansen, and even lengthier trips by more affordable modes of transportation.

Closing the Nagoya consulate would not likely have an immediate or significant impact on the lives of most American citizens living in the area, however. Passport renewal, the most commonly required government service by Americans living abroad, is already handled by mail, with no in-person, on-site renewal option available. Overseas voting for U.S. elections is also a by-mail only affair. As of last year, U.S. consulates and embassies in Japan no longer offer notarization services for “affidavits of competency to marry,” a form requested by the Japanese government when foreigners are getting married in Japan, and instead provides an online form that can be downloaded online stating that the U.S. government has no such certification system.

All of which is to say that many American expats can live in Japan for years, or even decades, without ever having to physically go to a consulate or embassy. Even for those who do need to visit a U.S. government office in-person, the U.S. Embassy and Consulates in Japan website already informs them that “The U.S. Consulate in Nagoya no longer provides American Citizens Services,” and directs them to the Osaka consulate instead.

As such, the Nagoya consulate’s role is more diplomatic liaison than service provider, facilitating cultural exchange and establishing ties with local educational, scientific, and business organizations.

▼ Recent posts from the U.S. consulate in Nagoya have highlighted chief consul Anna Wang visiting a Mitsubishi Heavy Industries facility in the city…

ワン首席領事が、名古屋市の三菱重工業大江工場を訪問し、民間機セグメントの皆さまと意見交換しました。ボーイング787「ドリームライナー」の主翼構造材「ウィングボックス」は、長年にわたりすべてここで製造されています。日米の航空宇宙産業パートナーシップを支える重要な取り組みです。… pic.twitter.com/xR4gRFNdA2

— 在名古屋米国領事館首席領事 (@USConsNagoya) July 21, 2026

▼ …and a visit to Nagoya by an American youth baseball team as part an international sister cities program.

7月12日、四日市ドームにてロングビーチと四日市のリトルリーグチームによる交流親善試合が開催されました！ 領事館からはアメリカ建国記念キャップとボールを提供し、1963年から続く両市の姉妹都市交流を祝いました。 日米の友情がこれからも続いていきますように！ pic.twitter.com/WthiUc370P

— 在名古屋米国領事館首席領事 (@USConsNagoya) July 14, 2026

So no, closing the Nagoya consulate is unlikely to trigger an immediate crisis for American expats in terms of accessing government services, nor will it bring an immediate halt to international cultural exchange. That said, it’s not going to make those things easier either, and it’ll be a sad development if the consulate does end up being deemed an unacceptable expense.

title: Yoshinoya gets into fancy fish, but is the cheap beef king reaching too far? [Taste test]
description: Japan’s biggest beef bowl chain is now serving up simmered kinmedai. When people think of Yoshinoya, they think of beef, and not just any beef, but cheap beef. That’s not to say Yoshinoya’s beef bowls are low-quality or bad-tasting, but the chain’s flagship fare is definitely more “good honest grub” than “fine dining.” So we […]
content:
Japan’s biggest beef bowl chain is now serving up simmered kinmedai.

When people think of Yoshinoya, they think of beef, and not just any beef, but cheap beef. That’s not to say Yoshinoya’s beef bowls are low-quality or bad-tasting, but the chain’s flagship fare is definitely more “good honest grub” than “fine dining.”

So we were surprised, and intrigued, when we found out that Yoshinoya is now also serving up fancy fish.

On July 27, Yoshinoya added the Gyu Kinmedai no Nizuke Teishoku, or Beef and Simmered Sea Bream Set Meal, to its menu. Kinmedai specifically is the Japanese name for the fish called splendid alfonsino in English, but no matter which moniker you use, it’s a premium variety of seafood, prized for its natural sweetness and satisfyingly substantial texture.

Finding the kinmedai set meal took a bit of sifting through the menu. The touchscreen terminal used for ordering at the Yoshinoya branch we visited didn’t mention the new item on its top screen, nor did we find it in the “limited-time specials” section. Instead, it was mixed in with the other options in the teishoku (定食) set meals tab. 899 yen (US$5.50) gets you a simmered kinmedai fillet, white rice, a bowl of miso soup, and a plate of Yoshinoya’s classic simmered beef which ordinarily tops its beef bowls. Alternatively, there’s a 799-yen version of the kinmedai set that skips the beef and gives you a plate of pickles in its place, but we opted for the full 899-yen set.

Size-wise, we were happy with the kinmedai fillet. Given how kinmedai isn’t something that’s even available at budget-friendly fast food restaurants, Yoshinoya only giving you a tiny sliver of the stuff wouldn’t have been a shock, but this was a decently sized slice, and a visually bountiful one too.

Most importantly, though, it was also a delicious slice of kinmedai! Slow-cooked in a traditional soy sauce-based simmer sauce, the fish is imparted with sweet and salty notes, and while it might not quite match what you’d get at a fancy seafood specialty restaurant or a portside eatery where the fish just came off the boat an hour ago, Yoshinoya’s kinmedai still has an excellent flavor. Basically, anyone who likes kinmedai will like this, and the fact that it’s available at such an accessible chain as Yoshinoya is incredible.

Though the fish is served on its own plate, we highly recommend letting some of the sauce drip onto the rice, since it’s so good that you won’t want to let a single drop go to waste.

Something has to be seriously tasty to make the beef in a Yoshinoya set meal feel like a supporting part instead of the main attraction, but that’s definitely what happens here. While this isn’t the very first time for Yoshinoya to serve up fish (they include salmon in some of their breakfast sets, for example), it is their first time to offer such a fancy fish as kinmedai.

So yeah, this is definitely worth digging through the menu to find. Just be aware that even though the Beef and Simmered Sea Bream Set Meal is listed with the regular set meals, it is in fact a limited-time item, though one without an announced specific ending date, so you’ll want to try it while you can.

title: Beautiful Totoro bonsai figure needs no watering, makes soothing rain showers whenever you want
description: Need a stress-soothing break? This figurine’s return means you can wait with Totoro while he waits for the Cat Bus. A bonsai tree can be a great way to add some picturesque tranquility to your home or work/study space. However, bonsai often require complex care routines, and if you don’t have much of a green […]
content:
Need a stress-soothing break? This figurine’s return means you can wait with Totoro while he waits for the Cat Bus.

A bonsai tree can be a great way to add some picturesque tranquility to your home or work/study space. However, bonsai often require complex care routines, and if you don’t have much of a green thumb, the hassle and stress of keeping one healthy can undo the sense of calm relaxation you were longing for.

So today let’s take a look at an alternative kind of bonsai that, in addition to being easier to care for, also has the major advantage of coming with Totoro.

Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku has restocked its previously sold-out My Neighbor Totoro Water Garden Bonsai, which carries the subtitle of “Kasayadori.” Kasayadori refers to taking shelter from the rain, especially under the boughs of a tree, and that’s exactly what Totoro is doing in this recreation of the scene from the anime movie where he’s waiting for the Catbus to come by.

The Totoro factor isn’t the only thing that separates this from a conventional bonsai tree, either, because this figurine can make its own weather.

Drawing power from an attached USB cord, the Water Garden Bonsai functions as a desktop fountain, with rivulets pouring down around Totoro and Mei.

The clever design means that once the water falls, it gets picked up in the base of the figurine…

…and cycled back up into the upper part to fall again, so there’s no need to refill it every time you want the soothing sound of rain.

Though big sister Satsuki is absent from the scene, Mei and Totoro are joined by a friendly frog, Soot Sprites in the tree branches, and a small Totoro with a leaf for an umbrella, who wobbles as the rain falls on him.

The fountain effect can be turned on and left to run indefinitely, or set to a “voice-activated” mode that will cause rain to fall for a five-minute cycle.

▼ A video showing the fountain turned in action

Unfortunately, the other Ghibli bonsai-style water gardens shown in the video are no longer available, but the Totoro Kasayadori version, which is 22 centimeters (8.7 inches) tall and priced at 17,600 yen (US$112) is once again available for order through the Donguri Kyowakoku online store here.

title: Japanese convenience store Lawson now has stir-fried noodle-cooking robot chefs
description: Lawson expands the territory of its robo chefs as they expand their menus. You can get plenty of hot meals at convenience stores in Japan, but they usually have a cold start. Head on over to the refrigerated shelves, and you’ll find an array of pre-made bento boxes, rice bowls, and noodle sets. Pick one […]
content:
Lawson expands the territory of its robo chefs as they expand their menus.

You can get plenty of hot meals at convenience stores in Japan, but they usually have a cold start. Head on over to the refrigerated shelves, and you’ll find an array of pre-made bento boxes, rice bowls, and noodle sets. Pick one out and take it up to the register, and after you’ve paid for it, it can be heated up in the store’s microwave.

But things are different now at certain branches of Japanese convenience store Lawson, where as of this month, you can get freshly stir-fried yakisoba noodles…that are cooked by a robot.

Tokyo-based tech company TechMagic’s I-Robo 2 has actually been cooking up meals at Lawson since the summer of last year, when it started out with fried rice and mixed vegetable stir-fry. It’s since expanded its repertoire, though and now can whip up yakisoba with pork, carrots, and cabbage.

▼ Lawson’s robo-cooked yakisoba

Because the machine can cook at higher temperatures than would be safe for a human chef (it stir-fries its fried rice at over 300 degrees Celsius [572 degrees Fahrenheit], for example), the cooking process is very speedy, taking only around 90 to 150 seconds.

And to be clear, this isn’t simply reheating or finishing off an already partially cooked dish. After you place your order, either via the in-store terminal, your phone, or directly at the register, a Lawson employee loads up the robot with the necessary ingredients for what you’ve selected, then packages your meal up for you when it’s ready.

Counting all the variations (with or without pork, regular or double-sized, and with or without fried chicken as topping for the fried rice), Lawson’s robo cook can prepare a total of 13 different dishes. Prices range from 499 to 1,099 yen (US$3.29 to US$7), a little on the high end compared to pre-made convenience store fare, but not bad for something freshly cooked to order.

The first Lawson with an I-Robo 2 cook was the Kita Otsuka Icchome branch in Tokyo’s Toshima Ward. The second was the Ebina Chuo branch in the town of Ebina, Kanagawa Prefecture, whose cooking robot was installed on August 6. The Yokohama Tarumachi Sanchome (Yokohama, Kanagawa) and Koto Shiomi Icchome (Tokyo) branches will be getting theirs on August 27 and September 17, and if they prove popular, expansion to even more branches will likely follow.

title: Starbucks Japan teams up with Traveler’s Company for new stationery and goods collection
description: Coffee and travel come together in a new range of exclusives by cult-favourite Japanese stationery brand. For coffee lovers, every sip is a journey, with new flavours and discoveries gradually revealing themselves along the way. So when Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo teamed up with Traveler’s Company, the Japanese stationery brand behind the cult-favourite Traveler’s Notebook, […]
content:
Coffee and travel come together in a new range of exclusives by cult-favourite Japanese stationery brand.

For coffee lovers, every sip is a journey, with new flavours and discoveries gradually revealing themselves along the way. So when Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo teamed up with Traveler’s Company, the Japanese stationery brand behind the cult-favourite Traveler’s Notebook, to create a limited-edition collection in 2019, the pairing proved to be so perfect that the two have continued releasing exclusive items together almost every year since.

▼ Making the tie-up even more special is the fact that both companies call Tokyo’s Nakameguro neighbourhood home.

This year’s collaboration between neighbours gives us five new products, based around the concept of “enjoying every day like a journey“, with designs inspired by Starbucks’ “Farm to Cup” philosophy and the Roastery Tokyo experience. All display the retro travel journal aesthetic that makes Traveler’s Company products so distinctive and popular.

▼ Starbucks Reserve Roastery Traveler’s Refill Tasting Notebook — 1,600 yen (US$11)

This special Traveler’s Notebook refill illustrates the coffee journey from farm to cup with letterpress printing and foil stamping. Inside are tasting note pages for recording coffees, meals, places visited, and memorable discoveries, allowing customers to create their own personal coffee journal.

▼ Starbucks Reserve Roastery Traveler’s Postcard Set — 2,000 yen

A set of six postcards featuring original illustrations of Roastery Tokyo icons and motifs by Traveler’s Company. Printed on a variety of textured papers, these are ideal for preserving memories of a visit or sharing handwritten messages from your travels.

▼ Starbucks Reserve Roastery Traveler’s Cotton Bag Medium — 1,800 yen

Inspired by the experience of bringing home a favourite coffee from a trip, this drawstring cotton bag is large enough to hold a bag of coffee beans, and also doubles as an organiser inside a larger bag.

▼ Starbucks Reserve Roastery Traveler’s Tote Bag — 5,000 yen

This canvas tote mimics the look of a well-travelled suitcase covered in souvenir stickers, with the Roastery Tokyo and Nakameguro being the prime destinations. Inside, you’ll find a large inner pocket that’s just the right size for holding a Traveler’s Notebook, as well as enough room to hold a tumbler or bottle, and other everyday essentials.

▼ Starbucks Reserve Roastery Traveler’s Handle Lid Stainless Steel Bottle (473 millilitres [16 ounces]) — 5,900 yen

Adorned in Roastery Tokyo-inspired travel motifs, this vacuum-insulated stainless steel bottle comes with a carry handle so you can easily carry it around with you on long journeys or even short strolls around Nakameguro.

Whether you’re a fan of Starbucks or Traveler’s Company, this is a collection that’s likely to sell out within days of its release. In a fitting twist, this range based around travel actually requires you to set out on a journey to find it, as it will be available exclusively at the Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo from 6 August.

title: Over 400 titles of free translated manga from publisher Shueisha available for a limited time
description: It’s their birthday, but we’re getting the presents! Shueisha is the publisher behind many of manga’s top titles, from One Piece and Naruto to Chainsaw Man and Demon Slayer. It’s also celebrating its 100th Anniversary this year, and planned something very big for the occasion called Manga Million, which starts today! The concept of Manga Million […]
content:
It’s their birthday, but we’re getting the presents!

Shueisha is the publisher behind many of manga’s top titles, from One Piece and Naruto to Chainsaw Man and Demon Slayer. It’s also celebrating its 100th Anniversary this year, and planned something very big for the occasion called Manga Million, which starts today!

The concept of Manga Million was to translate one million pages of manga into 100 languages. When we asked a PR firm representative for the project about how the translations were done, we were told “We have confirmed that no AI was used in the translation.”

Editor’s note: Following the publishing of this article, it has come to light that Flitto, a Japan-based company that bills itself as an “AI-powered translation service,” was contracted for Manga Million’s translation of One Piece into several dozen languages.

About 400 titles spanning shonen, seinen, shojo, and other genres will become available free of charge for a limited time in a vast array of languages. About 300 of these titles will be seeing their first-ever translations, so there’s sure to be something for just about every manga fan in existence here.

▼ Hopefully, East-Coast Canadian English is included, so I can read Kenshiro say, “Yer done fer, b’y. Just don’t know ‘er yet, eh?”

According to my new favorite President and CEO, Shueisha’s Hideaki Hayashi: “One of a publisher’s most important responsibilities is to connect creative talent with the public.” He adds that he hopes Manga Million “will create new connections with readers worldwide, provide opportunities to experience the richness and diversity of manga culture, and inspire future generations of manga creators.”

This was no small feat, even for a major publisher like Shueisha. In addition to coordinating with so many internal and outside parties, there’s also the hurdle of dealing with the vast international publishing deals that have been made over the years to allow this content to be provided for free everywhere.

And as a result, there is literally no catch to taking advantage of this hugely generous offering of manga. You can access it from any country around the world and don’t even need to register. The only condition is that you enjoy yourself, and I’m afraid that is non-negotiable.

I mean, I kind of wish there were some strings attached, because I’d have more to write about here, but it’s really just that simple. All you have to do is go to the Manga Million website and have fun. Maybe you can wish Shueisha a happy 100th birthday while you’re at it.

title: Kochia calling: Right now is a great off-season season to visit this beautiful Japanese park
description: Before Hitachi Seaside Park turns red for autumn, it’s got a beautiful summer color to show you too. Japan is a country with strong swings between its seasons, often resulting in splashes of color as different types of flowers or foliage reach their peak beauty. So if you’re headed to an outdoor attraction while traveling […]
content:
Before Hitachi Seaside Park turns red for autumn, it’s got a beautiful summer color to show you too.

Japan is a country with strong swings between its seasons, often resulting in splashes of color as different types of flowers or foliage reach their peak beauty. So if you’re headed to an outdoor attraction while traveling in Japan, timing is important, and right now is a fantastic time to visit Hitachi Seaside Park.

“Wait a second,” you might be thinking. “I though you guys said that early summer is a good time to visit that park, since that’s when its blue Nemophila flowers are in bloom. And wait, didn’t you say autumn is good too, because that’s when the park’s kochia bushes all turn red?” Yep, we sure did, but late summer is also awesome at Hitachi Seaside Park, because before those kochia can turn red, they need to grow green, and that’s what they’re doing now.

The park has a total of roughly 40,000 kochia plants, and they cover the Miharashi no Oka (“Lookout Hill”). While the ocean is visible from the top of the hill, it’s the topography itself that really catches the eye here, and the paths that wind up and around the slope let you surround yourself with greenery.

As an added bonus, Hitachi Seaside Park tends to be less crowded in summer than in the spring or fall. A big reason for that is no doubt the higher temperatures in summer, so you’ll want to bring a hat or parasol with you, but even those can lend a jaunty, fashionable look to photos you snap while strolling amongst the kochia, especially if you color-coordinate with your outfit or the blue sky above on a sunny day.

This year, the park has even planted more kochia at the base of the hill, in the section called Miharashi no Sato, which also has examples of traditional Japanese farmhouse architecture.

This year’s kochia are expected to have their bright green color from now through late September, after which they’ll start transitioning to autumn red. And if you’re looking for other reasons to visit Ibaraki, don’t forget that it’s got a great beginner-friendly mountain hike you can do plus the mysteries of Gama Land to experience.

content:
After years of this video game horror trying to eat us, it’s finally going to help us with our hunger instead.

The first foes that spring to mind when thinking about Resident Evil are, of course, the video game series’ zombie hordes. Zombies aren’t known for their speed or smarts, though, so as long as you can keep your confrontations with them to an individual basis, they’re pretty easy to outmaneuver and outwit.

Providing a much greater level of terror on a per-monster basis is the Licker. First introduced to the franchise in Resident Evil 2, the Lickers would be creepy enough with their freakishly long tongues, razor-sharp teeth, and exposed brains. What makes them even scarier, though, is that Lickers can stick to flat surfaces, helping them lie in ambush or stalk unsuspecting human prey. The very first Licker that appears in the series is encountered crawling along the ceiling of the Racoon City police station…and the newest Licker is ready to hide right on your back.

Thankfully, this Licker doesn’t want to eat you, and is instead here to feed you. While, as shown in the above photo, its paired shoulder straps allow it to be worn like a backpack, the original purpose of this wearable monstrosity is as a Universal Studios Japan popcorn bucket.

In recent years, USJ has been at least as committed to letting gusts step into the worlds of Japanese video games and anime worlds as they have Hollywood movies, and Resident Evil has been an enthusiastic partner with the park’s annual Halloween Horror Nights event. In addition to the Licker popcorn bucket, this year USJ will also be running a Resident Evil Requiem The Live horror maze attraction, in which fans can enter the abandoned Wrenwood Hotel where the most recent game’s FBI analyst Grace Ashcroft has gone missing. The search for Grace quickly goes sideways, though, with USJ promising “a suffocating sense of terror with nowhere to escape” as monsters attack from all angles, including above and below.

For those who want to dress the part, USJ will also be selling Racoon City Police Department uniform shirts and bags that can be worn as a waist pouch, shoulder bag, or cross-body bag.

▼ It’s unclear if the lack of trousers on offer is because of a relaxed dress code for the RPD, or because USJ doesn’t want to sell you garments that might get ruined if Resident Evil Requiem The Live scares you so badly that you pee your pants.

Pricing details haven’t been announced, but the Licker popcorn bucket will be for sale at the popcorn cart in front of the park’s Stage 22, and the RPD gear at the Cinema 4-D Store. They go on sale September 9 and will be available while supplies last (which may not be very long, considering how quickly some previous collaboration buckets have sold out). Resident Evil Requiem The Live, meanwhile, runs from September 11 to November 8, operating daily from 10 a.m. Note that the horror maze is limited to guests age 15 and up, though at least it doesn’t require you to sign a consent form like another part of USJ’s Halloween attractions this year.

title: Japan’s largest online flea market reminds users that selling used school swimsuits is prohibited
description: Even if they’ve been professionally cleaned, used school swimsuits are too dirty for this marketplace. Previously, for example, we’ve looked at the Mercari market […]
content:
Even if they’ve been professionally cleaned, used school swimsuits are too dirty for this marketplace.

Mercari is Japan’s largest online flea market, a place where individual sellers offer an extremely wide range of new and used items. It’s not just collectibles that Mercari deals in, either. Previously, for example, we’ve looked at the Mercari market for such niche products as ATM envelopes and curses.

That doesn’t mean that Mercari will allow the purchase and sale of any and everything on their site, though. On August 3, Mercari posted a statement that it does not allow the sale of used school swimsuits, of the type worn by Japanese elementary, middle, and high school students.

School swimsuits, or “school mizugi” as they’re called in Japanese, are usually nondescript black or navy-blue swimwear, shorts for boys and a one-piece bathing suit for girls, used during P.E. class swimming units. There’s often a space for the student to write their name on the garment, and some schools have the institution’s emblem printed on them as well.

▼ Mercari photo examples of new school swimsuits

Overall, though, school swimsuits are designed for functionality over fashionableness, and they’re so plain-looking that you’ll never really catch someone wearing their school swimsuit to the beach, public recreational pool, or anyplace else where they’re swimming for fun outside of their required educational curriculum.

As something that’s only going to be worn for a short time and in very specific circumstances, and the rate at which kids grow meaning that they probably won’t be able to use the same school swimsuit for two school years in a row, they might seem like the sort of thing that budget-pressed families would want to purchase used or sell off when no longer needed but still in usable condition. However, while not specifically mentioned by Mercari in its statement, there’s a certain segment of the Japanese population that has a less than wholesome interest in school swimsuits, viewing them through the same prurient lens that some people do school uniforms. For such would-be buyers, the desirability of a school swimsuit is tied to it having actually been used, and it’s understandable that Mercari doesn’t want to be part of the pipeline for such skeevy transactions.

So with hot summer weather here and demand up for swimwear in general, Mercari has posted a reminder that, even if they’ve been professionally cleaned, the site does not allow the posting of used school swimsuits for sale.

Mercari does allow users to sell/purchase used non-school swimsuits, including specialized competitive swimming suits, though they must be free of any written names of previous wearers or school emblems. The sale and purchase of new, unused school swimsuits is also allowed, though these too must not have any specific school’s crest or emblem.

Postings that are found to be in violation of the policy will be removed, and any sales that managed to slip through the cracks and be placed will be cancelled prior to shipping, with banning of the seller’s account also a possibility, as was also the case for Mercari merchants who tried selling Slime eyedrops and ultrasound photos.

title: Anime fan in Japan arrested for ordering and cancelling over 4.3 billion yen in anime merch
description: Shop ‘till you drop unfortunately becomes shop ‘till you get arrested. As any hard-core fan can tell you, anime and manga can be a pricey hobby. Sure, the proliferation of video streaming services and digital reader apps mean the content itself is much more affordable than it used to be, but the modern otaku merchandising […]
content:
Shop ‘till you drop unfortunately becomes shop ‘till you get arrested.

As any hard-core fan can tell you, anime and manga can be a pricey hobby. Sure, the proliferation of video streaming services and digital reader apps mean the content itself is much more affordable than it used to be, but the modern otaku merchandising industry is more robust than ever, with an endless flow of figures, plushies, character standees, and more for fans to covet.

This brings us to a 32-year-old restaurant worker living in Osaka’s Kita Ward, who, in a statement to the police, said “I like anime,” and has the numerical data to back it up. Over a roughly two-year period beginning around October of 2023, she ordered more than 4.3 billion yen (US$27 million) worth of items from manga publisher Shueisha’s Jump Character Store. If you’re wondering how she managed to pay for all that merch on what’s assumedly a modest food service worker’s salary, the answer is that she didn’t.

That’s not to say that the woman, Mayu Yoshida, stole anything. Instead, she placed the orders but never paid for, or took delivery of, the items. She did this through two methods, the first of which involved exploiting Japan’s convenience store prepayment system. For shoppers who either don’t have a credit card or don’t want to carry a balance on it, many online retailers in Japan allow customers to place an order but pay for it at a convenience store, with the seller shipping the item once payment has been confirmed. There’s a limit, though, to how much time is allowed to pass between the order’s placement and payment, after which the order will be cancelled. So Yoshida would order figures, key chains, and other items through the Jump Character Shop, select the convenience store prepayment method, and just never actually go to pay for them. Between 2024 and 2025, she placed orders with a total bill of over 4.3 billion yen this way.

Her second strategy was to order items from the Jump Character Shop and select the cash-on-delivery payment method, wherein the recipient renders payment to the delivery person. In these instances, Yoshida would refuse delivery, and therefore not pay for, the things she’d ordered. It’s unclear what the total value was for the orders she refused delivery of, but you have to wonder if any delivery person got tired of coming to her house again and again.

▼ Please, ma’am, I’m begging you, pay for this one.

As a major online retailer, the Jump Character Store likely has protocols in place to flag orders from shoppers who habitually cancel or refuse delivery of their orders, but Yoshida got around these safeguards by creating 238 different customer accounts and hopping from one to another.

However, just because she wasn’t keeping any of the items without paying for them doesn’t make this a no-harm, no-foul situation. By not paying for the COD items, she also wasn’t paying for the shipping charges, leaving Shueisha with a cumulative bill of approximately 7.5 million yen in fees for items sent to her which then had to be returned. There’re also restocking and order-processing costs involved, all of which were enough for the police to arrest Yoshida on charges of fraudulent obstruction of business, which she has admitted to, on August 4.

The repeated targeting of the Jump Character Store might make it seem like she has a bone to pick with the manga magazine or its publisher, but that’s actually not the case. “I have been feeling stressed from daily life, and I felt a sense of satisfaction and refreshment from ordering items before they sold out,” said Yoshida following her arrest. “I do not have any resentment towards Shueisha.”

A particularly bittersweet aspect to the situation is that Yoshida had previously been a legitimate paying customer with the Jump Character Store, placing her first order in the fall of 2018. Hopefully once her legal situation is sorted out she’ll be able to return to a more responsible form of fandom.

title: 7-Eleven Japan rethinks convenience store drinks with new Grilled Corn Chilled Soup Smoothie
description: Exclusive to only two wards in Tokyo, this is a must-try drink that’s very hard to get. content:
Exclusive to only two wards in Tokyo, this is a must-try drink that’s very hard to get.

We’re always on the lookout for new and unusual convenience store finds in Japan, so when 7-Eleven announced it would be releasing a never-before-seen chilled soup smoothie made with grilled corn, we knew it was something we had to try.

Finding it, however, proved to be more challenging than we’d thought, as it’s currently only available at select 7-Eleven stores in Tokyo’s Chuo and Chiyoda wards. After visiting four stores in Chuo without any luck, we eventually found it at our fifth stop, where a huddle of them were lying in wait like golden treasures, gleaming at us from inside the standing freezer section.

▼ A huddle sounds like a good collective noun for smoothies.

After plucking one out and paying for it at the register, we headed over to the smoothie machine at the counter, where we scanned the barcode on the lid before tearing it off to look inside.

▼ 冷製スープ = Chilled Soup

▼ There, in the cup, we found… actual pieces of grilled corn!

The corn looked good enough to eat right away but we were here to drink it, so we popped the cup into the machine and waited for it to work its magic. With apple and banana puree also in the mix, we were curious to find out what this soup-smoothie fusion would taste like, and when it was ready, we were fascinated by the way the corn had totally disappeared and become liquid, with tiny dark grilled flecks being the only evidence of its existence.

Taking a sip, it was clear that the corn was the star of the show. Coupled with fermented rice bran, made with lactic acid bacteria and yeast for gut health, and oligosaccharides to bring out the richness and sweetness of the vegetable, the corn flavour was sweet, with a subtle smokiness, making it different to the cans of corn potage that usually come to mind when we think of a Japanese-style corn soup.

While corn potage balances sweet and savoury flavours, this variety veers towards sweetness, which is apt seeing as it’s marketed as a smoothie. In fact, as we sipped our way through the drink, we found our taste buds becoming confused over whether this should be classed as a soup or a smoothie, as the grilled vegetable component made us think we were having soup, but the overriding sweetness made us think we were drinking a smoothie.

▼ Despite the addition of fruit puree, the smoothie doesn’t taste fruity at all, making it very different from all the other fresh smoothies at 7-Eleven.

At nearly 500 yen (US$3.19), it’s also one of the most expensive smoothies in the range, and one of the hardest to find, given its very limited availability. Though there’s no word yet on whether the smoothies will expand beyond the two Tokyo wards where it’s currently being sold, this is one of the chain’s most unusual and exciting creations, and well worth trying if you’re able to find it.

As part of 7-Eleven’s latest push to explore unexpected flavour combinations and challenge our expectations of convenience store food, this is a taste odyssey we’re happy to be on, and we can’t wait to see what weird and wonderful places the chain takes us with its next new release.
